intro: Karine Gilanyan plays the fifth of Rachmaninoff’s Op. 39 Études-tableaux, in E♭ minor and marked Appassionato. Its melody is set against repeated chords in the piano, and the study moves from a loud opening to a soft close in E♭ major.

sections.label: A · Melody above repeated chords
sections.mNote: Appassionato; the tune is marked molto marcato.

sections.label: B · Song over broken-chord accompaniment
sections.mNote: The left hand plays flowing sextuplets.

sections.label: A′ · Tempo I, melody in lower register
sections.mNote: Tempo I, pesante; repeated chords above a lower melody

sections.label: Coda · Broken chords, dolce melody
sections.mNote: The right-hand melody, marked dolce, moves towards E♭ major.

cues.title: Melody over triplet chords
cues.text: The marking is Appassionato, followed by molto marcato, strongly marked. Sustained upper notes sound above repeated triplet chords. Both hands are fully occupied, and the pianist has to sustain a single melodic line.
cues.evidence: Piano score, printed p. 63: Appassionato, molto marcato, sustained melody and chordal triplets. https://ks15.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/f/f5/IMSLP39591-PMLP01894-Rachmaninoff-Etudes-Op39.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Op. 39 and departure from Russia
cues.text: Rachmaninoff wrote the nine studies of Op. 39 in 1916–17, the last years he spent in Russia. Before the end of 1917 he left the country for good, and concert touring abroad later became his livelihood.
cues.evidence: Nigel Simeone’s Phillips Collection notes date Op. 39 to 1916–17 and place it before Rachmaninoff’s permanent departure after the October Revolution. The composer biography documents his subsequent touring career. https://www.phillipscollection.org/event/2016-11-12-vadym-kholodenko-0

cues.title: Left-hand sextuplets
cues.text: The repeated chords give way to sextuplets in the left hand. Above them, the right hand plays a melody in long notes, marked p.
cues.evidence: Piano score, printed p. 65, third system onwards: piano melody above left-hand sextuplets.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Letter to Respighi, 1930
cues.text: In a letter to Respighi of 2 January 1930 he named the pictures behind only five of his études: sea and seagulls, Little Red Riding Hood and the Wolf, a fair, an oriental march and a funeral march. This Appassionato is not among them, and no published letter explains the rest.
cues.evidence: Geoffrey Norris’s note for Hyperion CDA68188 (2018) quotes Rachmaninoff’s letter to Respighi of 2 January 1930, naming the pictures behind Op. 39 Nos. 2, 6, 7 and 9 and Op. 33 No. 7, and says his published correspondence gives no background for the other études-tableaux. https://www.hyperion-records.co.uk/dc.asp?dc=D_CDA68188

cues.title: Return of the opening, Tempo I
cues.text: At Tempo I, pesante the opening returns. The melody now lies in the left hand, below the repeated chords, and is again marked molto marcato. The right hand plays the repeated chords above it.
cues.evidence: Piano score, printed p. 68: Tempo I, pesante, lower melody marked molto marcato and repeated upper chords.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Return of the dolce melody
cues.text: The left hand returns to broken chords and the right hand takes up the melody again, marked dolce. Long notes sound above the accompaniment, and the dynamic drops through the closing pages.
cues.evidence: Piano score, printed pp. 69–70: quieter broken-chord accompaniment and the dolce melody on p. 70.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Close in E♭ major
cues.text: E♭ major replaces the minor key of the opening. The last page is marked morendo, dying away. Broken chords continue beneath the held upper notes until both hands stop.
cues.evidence: Piano score, printed p. 71: E♭ major closing harmony, ritardando, morendo and pp.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: Left-hand sextuplets begin
transitions.how: A diminuendo reduces the force of the repeated chords. The left hand begins sextuplets in the low bass, spreading the chord across the keyboard. After a short delay the right hand enters with a melody. Both hands are marked p.
transitions.evidence: Piano score, printed p. 65, second and third systems: diminuendo, low bass and piano sextuplet accompaniment.

transitions.title: Opening melody returns in the left hand
transitions.to: A′ · Tempo I, melody in lower register
transitions.how: The chords are marked accelerando with a crescendo, then ritenuto before Tempo I. At Tempo I the opening melody returns in the left hand, marked molto marcato, while the right hand repeats heavy chords. The bass descends to E♭.
transitions.evidence: Piano score, printed p. 68: accelerando, crescendo, ritenuto, Tempo I and pesante.

transitions.title: Right-hand melody returns over broken chords
transitions.from: A′ · Tempo I, melody in lower register
transitions.how: The right hand leaves its repeated chords and takes up the melody again. The left hand spreads the harmony into broken chords. The markings p and then dolce replace the instructions of the heavy return. The broken-chord figures continue through the closing pages, which move to E♭ major and end morendo.
transitions.evidence: Piano score, printed pp. 69–71: piano broken chords, dolce melody and E♭ major morendo ending.

composer.epithet: Russian composer and pianist who earned his living at the piano in exile and whose music uses the sound of the bells of his childhood.
facts: Zverev and Siloti at the piano; Taneyev and Arensky in composition

quote.text: I feel like a ghost wandering in a world grown alien. I cannot cast out the old way of writing, and I cannot acquire the new.
quote.source: Rachmaninoff to Leonard Liebling, 1939; published in The Musical Courier, 5 April 1943

composer.background:
“My hearty thanks to the old man for not having forgotten about me!” Rachmaninoff wrote to the singer Mikhail Slonov on 26 December 1892. The old man was Tchaikovsky, who had praised his opera Aleko in a newspaper interview. Rachmaninoff was nineteen and had recently graduated from the Moscow Conservatory with its Great Gold Medal. Tchaikovsky helped get the opera into the Bolshoi, and in May 1893 he sat in the audience and applauded.

His childhood had been less settled. He was born into a landowning family and grew up at Oneg, near Novgorod, until his father’s financial failures forced a move to St Petersburg. He entered the Conservatory there in 1883. His parents separated, his sister Sofia died of diphtheria, and his schoolwork went badly. His grandmother took him to Orthodox services, where he heard the choirs and bells he remembered all his life. In 1885 his cousin Alexander Siloti recommended that he move to Moscow to study with the piano teacher Nikolai Zverev, who was known for his strictness.
